sources: Mary Celeste: found 4 Dec 1872 by the Dei Gratia (Capt. David Morehouse) between the Azores and Portugal; left New York 7 Nov 1872 for Genoa with 1,701 barrels of (denatured) alcohol; 10 aboard: Capt. Benjamin S. Briggs, wife Sarah, daughter Sophia (2), 7 crew; ship seaworthy, ~6 months of food and water, crew's belongings left; lifeboat missing; one pump disassembled, sounding rod on deck, ~3.5 ft of water in the hold; last log entry 25 Nov 1872, 8 a.m., near Santa Maria (Azores); 9 barrels empty when unloaded in Genoa. Gibraltar Vice-Admiralty Court salvage inquiry 1873: no evidence of foul play. Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica; Smithsonian Magazine (2007, 'Abandoned Ship: The Mary Celeste'); Wikipedia 'Mary Celeste'.
Boston Post, 24 Feb 1873 (reprinted New York Times 26 Feb 1873): 'seized by pirates' – public domain clipping, Wikimedia Commons.
Arthur Conan Doyle, 'J. Habakuk Jephson's Statement', Cornhill Magazine, Jan 1884 (fiction, published anonymously; some readers took it as fact).

Most-cited explanation (abandonment in the yawl for fear of sinking/explosion) is a hypothesis; the fate of the 10 is unknown. Sea monster / 'something from the sky' = popular claims only, no evidence.
